issues.legal_issue: A statutory rent-control revision empowered the High Court to examine the propriety of the appellate authority’s order and was not confined to reviewing its legality.
material_facts: The matter came before the High Court in a revision from an appellate authority’s decision in an eviction proceeding.
The High Court stated that it could not reappraise the evidence unless the appellate finding suffered from a legal infirmity, and its approach to the evidence was influenced by that limitation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s revisional powers extended to examining the propriety, as well as the legality, of the appellate authority’s order; it had unduly restricted its approach.
issues.legal_principle: Section 15(5) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 authorizes the High Court to examine the legality or propriety of the order and to pass an appropriate order. Those powers are wider than, and are not akin to, the High Court’s revisional powers under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.rent_control_revision: The proceeding is a revision to the High Court from an order made in a rent-control matter.
predicates.revision_power_includes_propriety: The law governing the revision authorizes the High Court to examine whether the challenged order is proper, as well as legal.

issues.definition: When a rent-control revision is governed by a power to review propriety, the High Court may examine the propriety of the challenged order.

issues.legal_issue: A landlady’s bona fide need for residential premises for her own occupation was established where the evidence showed a genuine plan to return to her only home, and the contrary findings rested on erroneous factual assumptions and failures to account for her efforts to obtain possession.
material_facts: After her husband died, the landlady decided to leave rented accommodation and live in the only house she owned in the country, where she had lived for many years and had social connections.
She repeatedly asked the tenant to vacate, including through personal visits and letters, before filing the eviction proceeding.
The tenant admitted that the landlady had not demanded higher rent; her husband’s earlier letter seeking more rent had been written during his terminal illness.

The appellate authority relied in part on an assumption that the landlady had relet another floor of the house after her husband’s death, but the letting had actually been done by her husband while alive.

The High Court treated the time before filing the proceeding as unexplained delay despite the landlady’s efforts to obtain possession, and did not account for evidence that her own landlord was pressing her to leave her rented accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The landlady established a bona fide need for the premises; the appellate authority and the High Court were not justified in finding otherwise. The Supreme Court set aside their decisions and restored the Rent Controller’s eviction order.
issues.legal_principle: Section 13(3)(a)(i) of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 permits eviction where the landlady requires the premises for her own occupation. Whether that need is bona fide must be assessed on the evidence and surrounding circumstances; a finding based on an erroneous factual assumption or on ignoring material circumstances cannot stand. No earlier cases are relied on in the judgment.

rule.if: residential_eviction_proceeding and owner_plans_personal_occupation and premises_are_only_owned_home and owner_made_efforts_to_obtain_possession and no_enhanced_rent_demand and adverse_finding_rests_on_material_error

predicates.residential_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction from residential premises on the ground that the owner requires them for personal occupation.
predicates.owner_plans_personal_occupation: The owner has decided to live in the premises rather than merely expressing a wish to possess them.
predicates.premises_are_only_owned_home: The premises are the only home owned by the owner in the relevant country.
predicates.owner_made_efforts_to_obtain_possession: The owner made attempts to obtain vacant possession before pursuing eviction.
predicates.no_enhanced_rent_demand: The evidence does not show that the owner sought increased rent from the tenant as the real purpose of seeking possession.
predicates.adverse_finding_rests_on_material_error: The finding against the owner’s claimed need relies on an erroneous factual assumption or disregards material circumstances supporting the claim.

issues.definition: Where an owner seeking residential premises for personal occupation genuinely plans to live in the only home the owner owns, has tried to obtain possession, has not sought increased rent, and the adverse finding rests on a material error, the owner’s bona fide personal need is established.

issues.legal_issue: Evidence that the owner’s landlord had filed an eviction proceeding and served summons was relevant to corroborate pressure to vacate rented accommodation even though no eviction order had been passed.
material_facts: The landlady sought permission to produce additional evidence that her landlord had filed an eviction proceeding against her and served her with summons.
The High Court rejected the application because no eviction order had been passed.
The Supreme Court held that the filing of the proceeding and service of summons could corroborate the landlady’s evidence that she was under pressure to vacate her rented accommodation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to reject the evidence as irrelevant merely because no eviction order had been made; the evidence had probative value as corroboration.
issues.legal_principle: Order 41, Rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure governs applications to produce additional evidence. The absence of a final eviction order does not make evidence of a proceeding filed against the proposed witness or party, and service of summons, irrelevant when it corroborates claimed pressure to vacate.

rule.if: additional_evidence_request_in_eviction_appeal and landlord_filed_eviction_proceeding and summons_served_on_occupant and no_eviction_order

predicates.additional_evidence_request_in_eviction_: A party in an eviction appeal asks to produce additional evidence about pressure to leave rented accommodation.
predicates.landlord_filed_eviction_proceeding: The party’s landlord filed a proceeding seeking that party’s eviction from rented accommodation.
predicates.summons_served_on_occupant: The party received summons in the landlord’s eviction proceeding.
predicates.no_eviction_order: No final order requiring the party to leave had been made when the additional evidence was offered.

issues.definition: When an occupant offers evidence that the landlord filed an eviction proceeding and summons was served, that evidence is relevant to corroborate pressure to leave even if no eviction order has been made.
